title: Service introspection and client-adaptive contracts
author: Diego Morales
content:
Overview
--------
This document defines Redwood's standards for service introspection endpoints and a lightweight client-adaptive contract protocol. The goal is to allow clients and intermediate proxies to discover service capabilities, negotiate compatible request/response feature sets, and gracefully degrade when capabilities or performance constraints differ across deployments (hosted, dedicated, private).

Why this exists
---------------
- Reduce unexpected errors from silent capability mismatches (e.g., streaming vs non-streaming, structured-output modes).
- Make rollouts and multi-variant serving safer by enabling clients to detect and adapt to available runtime features.
- Provide a small public surface for build-time and run-time tooling (SDKs, health checks, traffic routers) to make informed routing and fallback decisions.

Scope
-----
Applies to: API surfaces implemented by Redwood core services that accept inference-style payloads (generation, chat, embeddings, reranking) and any service that must advertise runtime-level features (quantization profile availability, streaming, tool-calling support).
Does not apply to: internal-only debug endpoints or per-tenant configuration served exclusively via private control planes unless explicitly adopted.

Key concepts and definitions
----------------------------
- Capability Manifest: JSON document published at a well-known introspection endpoint describing supported features, versioning, and limits.
- Client Capability Vector: a set of capability labels and preferred fallbacks sent by a client to express expectations.
- Adaptive Contract: the negotiated, best-effort feature subset agreed for a request. Not a long-term API versioning mechanism; used to guide per-request handling.

Contract model (principles)
---------------------------
1. Self-describing endpoints: every public inference endpoint must expose a /.well-known/capabilities (or /v{n}/capabilities) endpoint returning the Capability Manifest.
2. Explicit negotiation: clients may supply X-Client-Capabilities (JSON or compact header) and Accept-Model-Profile headers to signal preferences. Servers MUST honor negotiation if they can, otherwise return the agreed subset and warnings.
3. Fail-open with guardrails: when features requested are unavailable, servers should return a structured warning object and a conservative fallback unless configured to reject the request.
4. Backwards-compatibility: introspection is an orthogonal layer — it helps avoid breaking changes but is not a replacement for proper API versioning.

Capability Manifest (reference schema)
-------------------------------------
The manifest is a small JSON document published on the same host as the service. The manifest SHOULD be under 8KB. Example fields (human-readable names included for clarity):

{
  "service": "redwood.inference.text",
  "version": "2026-11",
  "interfaces": ["generation", "streaming"],
  "features": {
    "structured_output": "1.2",
    "tool_calling": "stable",
    "kv_cache": "enabled"
  },
  "limits": {
    "max_tokens": 4096,
    "concurrent_requests": 32
  },
  "profile_hash": "sha256:abc123...",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-01T18:23:00Z"
}

Fields explained:
- service: canonical service name used in logs and routing.
- version: human readable release/timestamp identifier for the runtime capability set.
- interfaces: list of major supported interfaces (e.g., generation, streaming, embeddings).
- features: map of named capabilities to semantic version or state (alpha/beta/stable/enabled/disabled).
- limits: enforceable numeric limits (tokens, concurrency, payload_size_bytes).
- profile_hash: cryptographic fingerprint of server-side model/profile for quick compatibility checks.

Negotiation headers and semantics
--------------------------------
- X-Client-Capabilities: JSON string or base64-encoded compact vector listing prioritized features. Example: {"prefer": ["streaming", "structured_output"], "allow_fallbacks": true}.
- Accept-Model-Profile: a comma-separated list of accepted profile_hash prefixes. If no overlap, server returns 409 with an Adaptation-Options response (see below) unless configured to fallback.
- Expect-Fallback: boolean hint; when true, server should attempt a safe fallback rather than rejecting.

Server response patterns
------------------------
1. Full agreement: 200 OK, body as usual, no capability warnings. Response header: X-Agreed-Capabilities: compact-vector.
2. Fallback agreement: 200 OK, body produced with reduced features; header X-Agreed-Capabilities and X-Capability-Warning (structured JSON string) describing which features were downgraded.
3. Unacceptable mismatch: 409 Conflict with body containing Adaptation-Options: suggested feature set and recommended client action.

Adaptation-Options example (409 body)
-------------------------------------
- recommended_mode: "non-streaming"
- suggested_headers: {"X-Client-Capabilities": "{\"prefer\":[] ,\"allow_fallbacks\":true}" }
- estimated_penalty: "latency +120ms"

Client adaptation rules (SDK guidance)
-------------------------------------
1. Prefer negotiation first: call GET /.well-known/capabilities at SDK initialization and cache per-host for TTL=5 minutes by default.
2. Apply conservative defaults: if a feature is unknown, the client MUST not assume it exists.
3. On 409, automatically attempt the top adaptation option up to 2 retries with exponential backoff.
4. Surface warnings to the application when fallbacks are applied; do not swallow capability warnings silently.

Operational requirements and SLOs
--------------------------------
- Every production inference host must serve a Capability Manifest with latency < 50ms 95th percentile.
- Manifests should be invalidation-safe: if the manifest cannot be produced, respond HTTP 503 and set Retry-After with a short TTL.
- Logs: negotiation attempts and outcomes (agreements, fallbacks, conflicts) are emitted to telemetry with labels {service, client_id, outcome, reason}.
- Telemetry SLI: fraction of requests that required a fallback should be <1% for stable releases; flagged in the rollout dashboard if increasing.

Example: negotiation flow (numbered steps)
-----------------------------------------
1. Client calls GET https://inference.redwood.ai/.well-known/capabilities -> cached manifest.
2. Client issues POST /v1/generate with header X-Client-Capabilities: {"prefer": ["streaming"], "allow_fallbacks": true} and Accept-Model-Profile: "sha256:abc".
3. Server inspects manifest, matches streaming==false, responds 200 with non-streaming payload and X-Capability-Warning: {"downgraded": ["streaming"]}.
4. Client SDK emits a warning to app telemetry and optionally reroutes long-poll UX to progressive rendering.

Release and rollout playbook
---------------------------
- Any change to the manifest schema requires an ADR and a staged rollout:
  1) Draft change and update test harness.
  2) Canary: enable new manifest on 2% of traffic for 48 hours.
  3) Monitor fallback rate and error surge metrics.
  4) Roll forward to 25%, 50%, 100% if fallback rate stays within thresholds.
- For private deployments: document the feature flags that map to manifest entries and provide a migration checklist for customers.

Testing and validation
----------------------
- Unit tests: manifest serializer/deserializer roundtrip.
- Integration tests: simulator that runs client capability vectors against a set of manifests and asserts correct server responses.
- Synthetic tests: daily synthetic calls to /.well-known/capabilities for each region; alert on missing manifests or latency regressions.

Operational runbook (quick steps)
--------------------------------
1. Manifest missing -> check runtime-config service and generation job; restore from last-known-good and set maintenance flag.
2. Unexpected large number of fallbacks -> investigate recent rollout changes, kernel changes, or model swap. Revert if fallback rate > 3% sustained for 2 hrs.
3. Client incompatibility complaints -> collect client headers and profile_hashes; coordinate with SDK team to push compatibility patches.

Checklist for engineering owners
-------------------------------
- [ ] Expose /.well-known/capabilities on every public host.
- [ ] Emit negotiation telemetry.
- [ ] Add unit + integration tests to CI.
- [ ] Update SDK to consult manifest and use header negotiation.
- [ ] Document private-deployment mapping for customer AEs.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Owners: inference-platform (primary), sdk-team (secondary)
- Escalation: oncall-inference -> platform-lead -> head-inference.
- Docs + SDK work: assigned to Diego Morales.

Appendix: sample curl examples and JSON snippets
-----------------------------------------------
1) Fetch manifest
$ curl -fsS https://inference.redwood.ai/.well-known/capabilities

2) Client header (compact JSON)
X-Client-Capabilities: {"prefer":["streaming","structured_output"],"allow_fallbacks":true}

3) Server warning header example
X-Capability-Warning: {"downgraded":["streaming"],"reason":"streaming-disabled-on-host","advice":"use-progressive-render"}
